archived.answer: Archiving a species only takes it out of your lists and counts, it never deletes anything. Find it any time under <archivedLink>Settings, Archived species</archivedLink> and unarchive it.
archived.question: I archived a species by mistake. How do I get it back?

externalDrive.answer: No. Only register one if your library is actually split across more than one physical drive. If everything fits on your computer's own storage location, there's nothing to set up.
externalDrive.question: Do I need to register an external drive?

otherTaxa.answer: Yes, turn on "Search iNaturalist for other species" under <speciesLink>Settings → Species & Import</speciesLink>. After that, jumping to a species from the header search box will offer a "Search iNaturalist" option whenever there's no local match, searching by scientific name works best, then you pick which region it belongs to. It shows up under its own group (Insects, Fungi, Plants, and so on) on your Collection page, without rarity or occurrence data, since Lifer has no real dataset behind those groups yet.
otherTaxa.question: Can I add species for a group Lifer doesn't have a dataset for (insects, plants, fungi, and the like)?

rarity.badges: A species card can show two rarities. The plain badge ("Rare") is the worldwide rarity: how hard the species is where it's easiest to find. On a region's checklist a second badge ("Occasional here") is its rarity in that region, and "Rarity here" in Group and Sort uses it. Lifer rates each species against the most-reported species of its group in each province or state: eBird and GBIF sightings for birds, iNaturalist photos for mammals, reptiles, amphibians and fish. A country's rarity is its easiest well-surveyed province. Tap a rarity badge to see the numbers behind it.
rarity.common: <term>Common:</term> an everyday species, seen anywhere, anytime (House Sparrows, Mallards, crows).
rarity.endangered: Rarity isn't how endangered a species is: an endangered wader can be on every mudflat, and a species of no conservation concern can be legendary if it lives in one hard-to-reach spot. The IUCN status is shown beside the rarity instead. Where there are too few records or photos to tell, a species shows "Not enough data" instead of a guess. Marine invertebrates aren't rated yet.
rarity.intro: Rarity is how hard a species is to find and photograph in that place:
rarity.legendary: <term>Legendary:</term> once in a lifetime; very local or extremely elusive (a Wolverine, a vagrant far from home).
rarity.occasional: <term>Occasional:</term> findable with a little effort in the right habitat (an Osprey over a lake, a Great Blue Heron in a marsh).
rarity.question: What does the rarity (common, occasional, uncommon, rare, legendary) mean?
rarity.rare: <term>Rare:</term> needs travel and patience; getting a shot is a notable achievement.
rarity.tight: Common is kept tight on purpose, to genuine everyday species, so each rarity means something in the field instead of most species piling up at the easy end. The same species can be Common in one place and Occasional in the next: Great Blue Herons are on every Florida pond, but take a trip to the right marsh in most other states.
rarity.uncommon: <term>Uncommon:</term> needs a dedicated search; it won't turn up on a casual outing.

share.answer: On a server/self-hosted install, yes: group photos into an <albumsLink>Album</albumsLink> and share it as a public link, no account needed to view. You control whether the link requires a password, when it expires, and whether visitors can download the photos. Location data is never included in a shared link, even if you turn on the camera-info option. This isn't available in desktop mode, since a local install has no public address to hand out.
share.question: Can I share photos with someone who doesn't use Lifer?

undownloaded.answer: You can still search for a species by name, but its detail page will prompt you to download that region before showing reference photos or habitat info. That reference data is bundled into the region download rather than fetched on demand, so it only shows up once the region is downloaded from <regionsLink>Settings → Species and import → Species downloads</regionsLink>.
undownloaded.question: What happens if I open a region I haven't downloaded?

uploadPaths.answer: All three end up with the same organized folder structure, they're just different starting points. A species page's Import is for a photo (or a few) of one specific species. Import is for a big batch where you'll assign species one by one afterward. Trips is for a whole folder from an outing that references files in place rather than copying them in.
uploadPaths.question: What's the difference between importing on a species page, Import, and Trips?

library.drives: A library spread across several drives can register each one in <storageLink>Settings → Storage</storageLink>, and Lifer remembers which drive each photo is on. Most people never need this.
library.intro: Every original photo you import goes straight into your library's Storage location, grouped by animal group (Birds/Mammals/Fish/Other) then species, so your library stays usable outside Lifer too:
library.title: Your library structure
library.folderLayout: A different Folder layout files photos by year instead, under {folder} (each photo's own capture year, not the year you imported it), or by date, trip or place.

browse.body: The <galleryLink>Gallery</galleryLink> shows every photo you've taken across every species, searchable by species name, camera details (try "600mm"), or a natural-language description of what's in the shot ("fox playing", "bird eating"). Group your favorites into a named <albumsLink>Album</albumsLink>. On a server install, an album can also be turned into a public link to share, with an optional password and expiration. <statsLink>Stats</statsLink> breaks down your collection by gear, species, and year.
browse.title: Browse & organize

bulk.body: One species at a time is fine for a handful of photos, but for a whole session's worth, use <importLink>Import</importLink>. Drop in a batch of photos, assign a species to each one, and import them all together. That way you don't need to navigate to each species page one by one.
bulk.title: Import a whole session

raw.body: The quickest way for a whole session: on Import photos, open "Add RAWs to existing photos" and point "Choose a folder" at your whole SD card. Lifer matches each RAW to the JPEG you already imported from it, by file name and capture time, and files it under that species, with no species to pick. You can also drop RAWs in with their JPEGs in a normal import. A RAW that doesn't match anything is simply left alone on your card rather than guessed at. To keep a RAW you haven't edited yet, add it from that species' page with Import, then "Choose RAW files".
raw.title: Match RAW files

regions.body: Before anything else, go to <regionsLink>Settings → Species and import → Species downloads</regionsLink> and download the region(s) you'll actually be shooting in. A region only shows real reference photos and habitat info once it's downloaded.
regions.title: Download your regions

trip.body: Trips references an existing folder you have in place. It never copies or moves your photos. The <tripsLink>Trips</tripsLink> page lets you point Lifer at an entire trip folder, and re-scanning the same trip later picks up any new photos, and their matching RAWs, automatically. On a server install, the folder has to be inside the library folder or a folder the admin declared with LIFER_LIBRARY_ROOTS.
trip.folders: For this feature you'll want to organize the files into "Adjusted" and "RAW" folders so that the app knows where to look.
trip.title: Import a trip

upload.body: Browse to a region (or search directly), pick a species, and hit Import on its page. Or go to the Import page and bring in a batch of photos at once.
upload.counts: A species only counts as "photographed" once you've attached a real photo of your own. You can also mark a species as "seen" in case you didn't manage to get a photo. Photos will be automatically sorted into labelled folders in the directory of your choosing.
upload.title: Import photos of a species

import.title: Import photos
import.body: Add photos from a memory card or folder. Lifer suggests the species in each one.

collection.title: Collection
collection.body: Your life list: the species where you are, and the ones you've photographed.

gallery.title: Gallery
gallery.body: Every photo you've imported, with filters for species, place and date.

map.title: Map
map.body: Your photos on a map, placed where you took them.

albums.title: Albums and trips
albums.body: Gather photos into albums. A trip collects the photos from its dates.

stats.title: Stats
stats.body: Charts of what you've photographed, and where and when.

review.title: Review
review.body: Check the species Lifer suggested for your newest photos.

search.title: Search and shortcuts
search.body: Press {palette} to find any species, photo, place or setting. Press {shortcuts} to see every shortcut.

versions.title: Photo versions
versions.body: Edits, prints and exports of one photo stack together, so the photo counts once. To link one yourself, choose Versions in its ⋯ menu.
